title: Vocabulary
text:
The site follows the notation of the DPprior paper and of Broderick’s MLSS 2016 lectures, which use alpha for the concentration parameter. Her 2012 tutorial writes theta for the same quantity.








Term
Meaning on this site
Also written as




alpha
Concentration parameter of the Dirichlet process. In the Chinese restaurant process it is the pseudo-count of “tables not yet seen”: the n-th customer opens a new table with probability alpha / (alpha + n − 1).
theta (Broderick 2012)


Gamma(a, b)
Hyperprior on alpha with shape a and rate b, so E(alpha) = a / b.
—


J
Number of units whose effects or traits are modelled: sites, schools, studies, respondents.
N (Broderick; the number of customers)


K_J
Number of occupied clusters among the J units: the number of fitted components. E(K_J | alpha) = Σ alpha / (alpha + i − 1) ≈ alpha log J.
K_N (Broderick), “number of clusters”


components vs clusters
Components are the infinitely many atoms of the Dirichlet process; clusters are the components that at least one of the J units actually occupies. K_J counts clusters.
—


w_k
Population weight of component k (its share of the whole population).
rho_k (Broderick), pi_k


stick-breaking (GEM)
w_1 = V_1, w_k = V_k ∏_{j<k}(1 − V_j) with V_k ~ Beta(1, alpha). The order in which pieces are broken off is the size-biased order.
GEM(alpha)


size-biased order
The order in which clusters are met when units are drawn at random: large clusters tend to come first.
order of appearance


W_SB
Size-biased first weight: the population share of the cluster that a randomly chosen unit belongs to. W_SB | alpha ~ Beta(1, alpha), and under Gamma(a, b), Pr(W_SB > t) = (b / (b − log(1 − t)))^a. It is not the largest weight.
w_1 in size-biased order


W_max
The largest population weight. For t ≥ 1/2, Pr(W_SB > t) ≤ Pr(W_max > t) ≤ Pr(W_SB > t) / t.
—


rho
Co-clustering probability Σ_k w_k^2: the chance that two randomly chosen units share a cluster. E(rho | alpha) = 1 / (1 + alpha).
—


majority-mass dominance
Pr(W_SB > .5): a random unit belongs to a cluster holding more than half of the population.
dominance


extreme dominance
Pr(W_SB > .9): a random unit belongs to a cluster holding more than 90% of the population.
—


Proposition 1 band
For t ≥ 1/2, S(t) ≤ Pr(W_max > t) ≤ min(1, S(t) / t) with S(t) = Pr(W_SB > t); the size-biased tail is a lower bound for the largest-weight tail.
—


collapse
K_J = 1: all units in one cluster. Always said as a prior statement, Pr(K_J = 1), or a posterior one, Pr(K_J = 1 | data).
—


CRP
Chinese restaurant process: the sequential seating rule that generates the partition of the J units.
Pólya urn (Hoppe urn)


DP, DPM
Dirichlet process; Dirichlet process mixture (the model in which each cluster has its own effect or trait distribution).
DPMM



Terms such as size-biased weight, dominance, the Proposition 1 band and prior versus posterior collapse come from the DPprior paper; they do not appear in Broderick’s tutorials. The CRP, stick-breaking and GEM terms follow Broderick. K_J always counts fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units.

title: The unintended prior
text: An analyst who expects “about five groups” among J = 50 sites can calibrate a Gamma hyperprior on the concentration parameter to that judgment. Gamma(1.60, 1.22) does it: its implied number of clusters has mean 5.05 and SD 3.06, matching a negative-binomial target with those moments. The same hyperprior also fixes the sizes of the clusters, and there it says something the analyst probably did not intend.

title: The unintended prior
text:
Two readings of one prior

Count view (Panel A). The bars are the prior distribution of K_50, the number of occupied clusters among the 50 sites: mean 5.05, median 4, 90% interval [1, 11]. The circles are the negative-binomial target with the same mean and SD.
Weight view (Panel B). W_SB is the population share of the cluster that a randomly chosen site belongs to. Its tail is closed-form, Pr(W_SB > t) = (b / (b − log(1 − t)))^a: .487 above one half and .183 above .9.
In Chinese-restaurant language: pick one of the 50 sites at random; with probability .49 it sits at a table that holds more than half of the whole population. “About five clusters” and “one cluster holds most of the mass” hold at the same time.

Set a = 1 and b = 1 (the “vague” default) and the tails move to .591 and .303. Change J and watch the count view move while the weight view does not: the weight tail involves only a and b.






K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units. These are prior quantities. W_SB is not the largest weight; Pr(W_max > .5) is bounded between Pr(W_SB > .5) and twice that value (Proposition 1 of the paper).



Standalone version: embed/unintended-prior.html, for example ?a=1&b=1&J=100.

title: Other defaults: flat, diffuse and objective priors
text: Four more families of default hyperpriors, each chosen to look uninformative (or stable) in one sense and each informative in another. The Gamma numbers on this page are recomputed in the browser; the Jeffreys and Stirling-gamma priors, which are not Gamma, are integrated in R.

title: Other defaults: flat, diffuse and objective priors
text:
Quasi-degenerate Gamma(eps, eps)
Setting a = b = eps gives a Gamma with mean 1 and variance 1 / eps. As eps shrinks the prior approaches p(alpha) ∝ 1 / alpha and looks flat on the log scale, which is why Gamma(0.001, 0.001) became a reference default (Escobar and West, 1995, let a and b go to 0; BUGS uses Gamma(0.001, 0.001)). The flat stretch runs off toward alpha = 0, where every unit shares one cluster.






At eps = 0.037 (the SCAL shortcut at m = 100, rounded) a third of the prior mass lies below alpha = 1e-12 and P(K_100 = 1) = .834: the prior is 83% sure that all 100 units form one cluster.
At eps = 0.001, 97% of the mass lies below alpha = 1e-12 and P(K_J = 1) = .992 for J = 50, 100 and 500 alike.
The prior that looks least informative about alpha is the most informative about K.

title: Other defaults: flat, diffuse and objective priors
text:
K_n-diffuse priors
In the 1990s the Gamma was chosen by eye so that K_n spread over a wide range at the study’s n: Gamma(5, 0.5) at n = 74 (West and Escobar, 1993) and Gamma(3.5, 0.5) at n = 53 (West, Müller and Escobar, 1994); Vicentini and Jermyn (2025) illustrate the idea with Gamma(10, 1). Drawn on the relative axis k / n, the same prior is wide at one n and narrow at another.




Gamma(5, 0.5) at n = 74: E K = 21.0 with a 90% interval of [11, 32], the “wide range” it was chosen for. Gamma(10, 1) covers [5, 9] of 10 units but [15, 34] of 100.
The large E(alpha) (7 to 10) that spreads K rules out a dominant cluster: Pr(W_SB > .5) = .013 for Gamma(5, 0.5) and .005 for Gamma(10, 1), against .591 for Gamma(1, 1). Diffuse in K means extreme in the weights.
There is no rule behind the choice, so nothing tells you what (a, b) to use at another n.

title: Other defaults: flat, diffuse and objective priors
text:
The Jeffreys prior against DORO
Rodriguez (2013) proposed the Jeffreys prior for alpha: p(alpha) proportional to the square root of the Fisher information of the partition at n units. It depends on n and on nothing else, which makes it “objective” in one sense; DORO’s flat target on the number of clusters is “objective” in another. The two disagree.




At n = 100 the Jeffreys prior implies a K_100 that is symmetric about n / 2: P(K = 1) = .054 (all units in one cluster) and P(K = 100) = .054 (every unit alone), five times the flat 1/100, over a nearly flat floor near .007. Its mean, 49.8, is close to the flat target’s, but its ends are not. DORO’s best Gamma, for its part, spikes at 1 and humps near 90.
Its tail in alpha falls off like alpha^(−3/2), so it has no finite mean, and 4.3% of the prior mass lies above alpha = 1e4. That mass matters: a grid cut at alpha = 1e4 reports E K_100 = 47.6 instead of 49.8.
Neither prior allows much dominance: Pr(W_SB > .5) = .132 for Jeffreys at n = 100 (.302 at n = 10) and .088 for DORO’s fit.

title: Other defaults: flat, diffuse and objective priors
text:
The Stirling-gamma prior against Gamma(2, 4)
Zito, Rigon and Dunson (2024) built a prior on alpha that keeps the expected count where you put it: the Stirling-gamma Sg(a, b, m) has E(K_m) = a / b exactly at its reference size m. With m = n it pins E K_n at every n, where the Gamma(2, 4) they compare with drifts. It is the one existing prior that is count-stable across designs; the paper did not compare it, and its weight implications were not reported.




Counts. Sg(4, 1, n) and Sg(1, 0.25, n) keep E K_n = 4 from n = 10 to 2000. Gamma(2, 4) gives 2.86 at n = 50, 3.20 at 100, 4.35 at 1,000 and 5.51 at 10,000.
Weights. To hold the count at 4 as n grows, the Sg prior moves alpha toward 0, and the chance that a random unit sits in a majority-mass cluster rises: for Sg(4, 1, n) from .31 at n = 10 to .64 at 100 and .77 at 2000. Gamma(2, 4) keeps .726 at every n. Pinning one lens moves the other.







Prior statements only; K_J (K_n) is the number of fitted components among the J (n) units. The quasi-degenerate and K_n-diffuse read-outs repeat their moments with twice the alpha quadrature nodes; the change is below 1e-13. The Jeffreys prior is not a Gamma: its values and the Stirling-gamma values are integrated in R over the whole alpha line (r-export/06_jeffreys_sg_grid.R, n = 10 to 2000 for Sg). Rodriguez (2013) is cited through Vicentini and Jermyn (2025, Sec. 3.1.4), not from the original. Other sources: Escobar and West (1995); West and Escobar (1993), through Vicentini and Jermyn (2025, footnote 1); West, Müller and Escobar (1994), through Dorazio (2009).

title: The method map
text: Each rule on the previous pages answers one question. Put them all on one plane, the expected number of clusters E K_J against the chance Pr(W_SB > .5) that a randomly chosen unit sits in a cluster holding more than half the units, and a pattern appears: the corner of few clusters and little dominance is nearly empty.

title: The method map
text:
One plane for every prior






At J = 100: Vague Gamma(1, 1) sits at (4.84, .591), Gamma(2, 4) at (3.20, .726), DORO-Unif at (4.99, .547), the tabulated SCAL prior at (4.74, .654), SSI-Weight at (10.05, .250), the count-only TSMM calibration at (5.00, .557) and the Dual-Anchor at (6.65, .399).
The corner. The shaded box holds what the vocabulary target asks for (E K_J between 2 and 10) together with the Dual-Anchor’s weight bound (Pr(W_SB > .5) ≤ .40). At J = 100 three priors are inside: the Dual-Anchor (6.65, .399), and two that aim at more clusters, the SSI exemplar Gamma(1.81, 1.04) (7.26, .395) and DORO-Unif with mu_K = 10 (9.91, .284). At J = 500 only the Dual-Anchor is left. Priors that target the count alone land above the box; priors that target the weights alone drift out to the right as J grows.
J moves points sideways only. For fixed (a, b) the weight tail does not depend on J, so changing J slides every point left or right; SSI-Weight moves furthest (8.21 at J = 50, 14.47 at J = 500), because its E(alpha) = 2.8 is the largest of the labelled priors.
Hover or choose a prior to see its count distribution and W_SB density, and send its (a, b) and J to the Gamma(1, 1) dashboard (M-07).

title: The method map
text:
Transported versus recalibrated
A count judgment such as “about 5 clusters, between 2 and 10 with 80% probability” can be calibrated once and reused, or calibrated again for each design. Calibrated at J = 500 (the vocabulary study) it gives Gamma(2.1062, 3.0789); the figure shows what happens either way.




Carried unchanged, Gamma(2.1062, 3.0789) no longer says “about 5” at other sizes: it expects 2.36 clusters at J = 10, 3.43 at 50 and 3.90 at 100, reaching 5.00 only at J = 500.
Recalibrated at each J, the expected count is 5.00 everywhere the target can be met (J = 15 and up; at J = 10 no Gamma prior has this mean and variance), with the same 90% band [1, 11]. But the weights move: Pr(W_SB > .5) is .495 at J = 50, .555 at 100 and .652 at 500, because a larger design needs a smaller alpha for the same count.
The same count judgment therefore implies more dominance in larger designs. This is what the Dual-Anchor controls explicitly.







Prior statements only; K_J is the number of fitted components among the J units. Gamma and fixed-alpha points are recomputed in the browser; the Jeffreys and Stirling-gamma points come from R (r-export/02_methods_catalog.R). TSMM and Dual-Anchor are the paper’s J = 100 calibrations (OSM Table F.4), kept fixed when J changes. The recalibrated priors are TSMM fits by DPprior 2.0.0 (r-export/03_recalibrate_by_J.R); they agree with the paper’s Fig. 2 data.



Standalone versions: embed/method-map.html (for example ?J=500 or ?preset=headline) and embed/transported-vs-recalibrated.html (for example ?J=100 for the reference J, ?preset=noband).

title: DORO: a flat count target the Gamma cannot reach
text:
Dorazio (2009) asked for the least informative prior on the number of clusters and answered with a flat one: every K_n from 1 to n equally likely. No Gamma(a, b) hyperprior on alpha can deliver that, so DORO takes the Gamma whose implied count distribution is closest to flat in Kullback–Leibler divergence. The explorer solves that problem live for each n.





What to look for:

The target is out of reach. With two parameters the closest a Gamma hyperprior gets to a flat line is a spike at a single cluster (its shape a < 1 puts mass near alpha = 0) plus a hump near 0.9 n (the mass at large alpha), sagging below the target in between. At n = 10 the solution is Gamma(0.525, 0.046) with KL = .019, Dorazio’s own table entry; at n = 50 it is Gamma(0.467, 0.0068) with KL = .0705.
The gap grows with n and b goes to 0. The KL divergence rises from .005 at n = 5 to .095 at n = 100 while the rate b falls toward 0, so E(alpha) = a / b grows. For Dorazio’s fish data (n = 53) the solution is Gamma(0.465, 0.0063): E(alpha) = 73 and E K_53 = 28.4.
“Noninformative” is a strong statement. The prior now expects about n / 2 clusters among n units (E K_n near n / 2) and no dominant cluster (Pr(W_SB > .5) = .11 at n = 53), while every fixed Gamma prior grows like log n.
DORO-Unif (the paper’s variant) aims at a flat target on 1 to 2 mu_K − 1 instead. At J = 100 and mu_K = 5 the best Gamma is Gamma(2.43, 2.46), a single right-skewed hump: it still puts .070 on a single cluster, leaks .073 beyond 9, and gives Pr(W_SB > .5) = .547.







Prior statements only; K_n is the number of fitted components among the n units. Every (a, b) is solved in the browser by doroKL (Nelder–Mead on log a and log b, the same problem r-export/05_golden_v2_solvers.R solves in R; parity against verification/golden/solvers.csv). The two curves under the chart are solved at n = 5, 10, …, 100 after the page loads.



Standalone version: embed/doro-explorer.html (for example ?n=53, or ?preset=unif10 for DORO-Unif with mu_K = 10).

title: Worked example: J = 50
text:
An analyst expects about five clusters among J = 50 sites, with medium confidence (VIF 2.5, so sigma_K^2 = 2.5 × (5 − 1) = 10). The DPprior workflow runs four steps.






State. mu_K = 5, sigma_K^2 = 10 for K_50.
Calibrate (TSMM). Stage 1 uses a shifted negative-binomial proxy and starts at Gamma(2.667, 2.608), whose implied moments (4.415, 5.618) miss the target. Stage 2 solves the exact moment equations by Newton steps and returns Gamma(1.4082, 1.0770): E K_50 = 5.00, Var 10.00, median 4, 90% interval [1, 11].
Diagnose. The same prior gives Pr(W_SB > .5) = .497: a randomly chosen site has nearly even odds of sitting in a majority cluster. That is above the .40 trigger.
Decide. Dual-Anchor picks the largest weight on the count target (lambda = .30 on a 29-point grid) whose tail is at most .40: Gamma(2.3158, 1.4204), with E K_50 = 5.88, 90% [2, 12] and Pr(W_SB > .5) = .398. A hard bound of .25 is reported separately as a sensitivity analysis: Gamma(5.2745, 2.3059), E K_50 = 7.49, 90% [3, 13].

Turn on Show the Stage 1 initializer to see why Stage 2 is needed.






K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units. Pr(W_SB > .5) is a prior probability about the size-biased weight, not about the largest cluster. Exact Gamma parameters come from the replication package; the widget recomputes every number with the site’s engine.



Standalone version: embed/worked-example.html (?preset=da, ?preset=hard, ?preset=init).

title: Confidence moves the tails, not the middle
text:
The elicited mean is the same in every row, “about 5 clusters among 100 units”. Only the confidence changes, through the variance inflation factor: sigma^2 = VIF (mu_K − 1), so VIF 1.25, 1.5, 2.5 and 5 ask for a variance of 5, 6, 10 and 20.






The prior on alpha widens. From VIF 1.25 to 5 the calibrated prior goes from Gamma(7.13, 7.41) to Gamma(0.62, 0.56): its mean stays near 1 (0.96 to 1.11) but its spread grows.
The mean drives majority dominance. Pr(W_SB > .5) moves only from .53 to .61.
The variance drives extreme dominance and collapse. Pr(W_SB > .9) moves from .15 to .36, and the mass near zero, Pr(alpha < .1), from 0 to .18: a low-confidence count target quietly allows one cluster to take almost everything.
The two-lenses panels (C-04) show the same prior as a count distribution and as a weight distribution; J changes only the count.







Every row is solved in the browser by TSMM (dp-core tsmmFit) and matches the paper’s Table 2 and OSM Table F.4 (checked against DPprior 2.0.0 on the parity page). The lens panels are the widget of One alpha, two lenses, reused unchanged.









In DPprior Studio. For a whole grid of target means and confidence levels at once, use the Sensitivity panel of DPprior Studio, the Shiny app that accompanies the package (built on DPprior 1.1.0; it may take a moment to wake up). This site does not rebuild what Studio already does.



Standalone version: embed/vif-sensitivity.html (for example ?preset=5).

title: TSMM in the browser, checked against R
text:
Every calibration on these pages is solved in your browser by the site’s engine (dp-core). The table checks it against the DPprior R package (version 2.0.0): ten targets, from the paper’s J = 50 worked example to the three applications, plus one target that has no Gamma solution at all.






Two-stage moment matching (TSMM). Stage 1 starts from a closed form (A1): for J = 50 and the target E K = 5, Var K = 10 it gives Gamma(2.667, 2.608). Stage 2 runs Newton on (log a, log b) until the prior’s exact count mean and variance hit the target: Gamma(1.4082, 1.0770) after five steps, the same path the R package takes.
Agreement. All nine feasible targets agree to about 3e-8 on a and b (the tolerance is 5e-3), including STAR (5.134, 4.939), Bangert-Drowns (1.145, 1.221) and the vocabulary study (2.1062, 3.0789).
An impossible target. “Between 3 and 10 with 95% probability” at J = 100 asks for a count variance of 3.19, but every prior with E K = 6.5 has a variance above 4.52 (the point mass at alpha = 1.386). Both engines report that no solution exists, and the browser does so before any Newton step.







Golden values: verification/golden/tsmm_fits.csv, written by r-export/05_golden_v2_solvers.R with DPprior_fit(method = "A2-MN") (DPprior 2.0.0, loaded with pkgload::load_all); the parity run (verification/run_parity.mjs) checks the same rows on every build.

title: Where a Gamma prior exists
text:
Not every count target has a Gamma hyperprior. At J units, a target mean mu_K for K_J (the number of clusters) allows only a band of variances. Mixing over alpha always adds variance, so no Gamma prior can be tighter than the point mass alpha* whose mean count is mu_K. That is the profile bound v_J(alpha*), the red curve. Above the grey curve no count on 1..J has the variance at all: the curve is the count that puts all its mass on 1 and J.






The [3, 10] example at J = 100. “Between 3 and 10 clusters with 80% probability” is the target (6.5, 7.46), inside the band: Gamma(6.82, 4.82). The same interval at 95% is (6.5, 3.19), below the red curve, which passes 4.52 at mu_K = 6.5 (alpha* = 1.386). No Gamma prior has that little variance, so TSMM reports “no solution” rather than a poor fit.
The bound moves little with J. At mu_K = 6.5 the smallest variance is 4.20 at J = 50, 4.52 at J = 100 and 4.91 at J = 500; the ceiling grows with J.
Near the red curve the prior is almost a point mass. Within about .002 of the curve the solution has CV(alpha) < .01 (the gold edge). TSMM still finds that exact solution, with a large shape a, and labels it nearly a point mass.
Near the grey curve the solution runs to a and b near zero. TSMM converges up to about 95% of the ceiling; closer than that, b falls below 10^-17 and Newton stops without converging. Such targets say “anything from one cluster to J clusters”, which is rarely meant. The ceiling itself is reached only by a count split between 1 and J, never by a Gamma prior.

The same check runs inside the calibrator and the elicitation form, which also name the widest probability or smallest VIF that would work.






Curves from dp-core profileBound (bisection for alpha, then v_J(alpha)); fits from tsmmFit. The bound for [3, 10] at 95% matches an independent R computation (uniroot on the conditional mean, verification/golden/tsmm_fits.csv) to 1e-9; see the parity page.



Standalone version: embed/feasibility-map.html (for example ?preset=i95 or ?J=500&mu=5&var=10).

title: The Dual-Anchor frontier
text:
TSMM matches the count target exactly, but at J = 50 its prior still gives Pr(W_SB > .5) = .497: about half the time, the cluster of a randomly chosen unit holds most of the population. The Dual-Anchor refinement adds a second anchor on the weights and weighs the two with lambda (lambda = 1 is TSMM). Lowering lambda buys less dominance with more clusters.






The rule. Take the largest lambda whose prior is at or below the .40 trigger. At J = 50 that is lambda = .30: Gamma(2.3158, 1.4204), with Pr(W_SB > .5) = .398 and E K_50 = 5.88. Every larger lambda (grey) leaves the trigger on.
The price. Moving from TSMM (.497, E K 5.00) to lambda = .30 costs about 0.9 expected clusters. The hard bound .25, Gamma(5.2745, 2.3059), costs 2.5 (E K 7.49). It is reported as a sensitivity analysis, not as the recommended prior.
In the applications the hard bound can collapse to nearly a point mass: for STAR and Vocabulary it puts almost all prior mass at alpha = 2 (a above 3 million), where Pr(W_SB > .5) is (1/2)^2 = .25 to three decimals.

For the whole J = 50 workflow on one page, see the worked example; to see where the trigger comes from, see the elicitation form.






Grid: data/released/dual_anchor_grid.json (29 values of lambda; CC BY 4.0). Hard bound: data/precomputed/worked_example_j50.json. Applications: data/released/app_priors.json. Every probability and expected count on this page is recomputed with dp-core.









In DPprior Studio. To set the weight anchor as a quantile or a mean of W_SB rather than a probability, use the Dual Anchor panel of DPprior Studio, the Shiny app that accompanies the package (built on DPprior 1.1.0; it may take a moment to wake up). This site does not rebuild what Studio already does.



Standalone version: embed/dual-anchor-frontier.html (for example ?preset=hard or ?preset=0.5).

title: Calibrate a count target
text:
State what you expect about the number of clusters K_J among your J units, as a mean and a variance (or a variance inflation factor, VIF: sigma^2 = VIF (mu_K − 1)). The calibrator finds the Gamma(a, b) hyperprior on alpha whose implied K_J has exactly that mean and variance.






The J = 50 example. “About 5 clusters”, with VIF 2.5 (sigma^2 = 10), gives Gamma(1.4082, 1.0770) after five Newton steps from the closed-form start (2.667, 2.608).
The applications. STAR (J = 79, “between 2 and 8 with 80% probability”, sigma^2 = 5.48) gives Gamma(5.134, 4.939); Table 2 of the paper (J = 100, VIF 2.5) gives Gamma(1.666, 1.646).
When there is no answer. “Between 3 and 10 with 95% probability” at J = 100 asks for a variance of 3.19 around a mean of 6.5, but no Gamma prior with that mean has a variance below 4.52. The calibrator says so instead of returning a poor fit. A variance at or above (mu_K − 1)(J − mu_K) is refused too: no count on 1..J with that mean can reach it.
Just above the bound. A target a little above the smallest variance still has an exact answer, with a very large shape a: the prior is nearly a point mass (CV(alpha) below .01). The calibrator shows the mean and variance it achieves beside the target; a result that misses the target by more than 10^-6 is labelled approximate, never calibrated. Try ?J=50&mu=5&var=3.2219.
The weights come along unasked: check Pr(W_SB > .5) in the read-out, and see the J = 50 worked example for what to do when it is too high.







Solved by dp-core tsmmFit in the browser; checked against DPprior 2.0.0 on the parity page. K_J is the number of fitted components among the J units.



Standalone version: embed/tsmm-calibrator.html (for example ?J=79&mu=5&var=5.48).

title: From the Hoppe urn to stick-breaking
text: Put one black ball of mass alpha in an urn. Draw a ball with probability proportional to its mass. If it is the black ball, put it back together with a ball of a new colour. If it is a coloured ball, put it back with one more ball of the same colour. After n draws there are n coloured balls, and the chance that the next draw brings a new colour is alpha / (alpha + n). This is Hoppe’s urn, and it is the Chinese restaurant process with colours for tables.

title: From the Hoppe urn to stick-breaking
text:
What to try

Step (or Enter) a few times and follow the step strip: the first draw must take the black ball, so the first colour appears at once.
+100, auto. The colour shares stop moving much after a few hundred draws. The bar is one draw of stick-breaking weights, in the order the colours appeared (the same colours as the stick-breaking widget).
Repeat 1000 times. A thousand fresh urns: the first colour’s share lines up with the Beta(1, alpha) density. That is the first stick-breaking piece, and the share of the cluster a randomly chosen unit belongs to, W_SB, has the same Beta(1, alpha) distribution given alpha.
alpha. A small alpha keeps one colour dominant; a large alpha keeps opening new ones.







After Broderick (MLSS 2016, part II); the mathematics is re-implemented and no code is copied.



Standalone version: embed/hoppe-urn.html, for example ?alpha=0.5&n=200.

title: Paintbox: components versus clusters
text: Take a Dirichlet draw with many components and a small parameter: K = 1000 and a = 0.01. Lay its weights side by side on the unit interval. A handful of pieces are wide and the rest are slivers too thin to see. Now drop points uniformly on the interval, one unit at a time. Each drop lands in some piece; the pieces that have been hit are the clusters, and there are far fewer of them than components.

title: Paintbox: components versus clusters
text:
What to try

Drop 1, Drop 10, Drop 100. After 100 drops only a couple of dozen of the 1000 pieces are blue (the exact expectation for K = 1000 and a = 0.01 is 24.2). The staircase below records, for every drop, whether it hit a piece seen before or a new one; the steps get further and further apart.
log x. On a log scale of the drop number the staircase is close to a straight line: clusters grow like alpha log N, with alpha = K·a.
K and a. Keep K·a fixed (say K = 5000 and a = 0.002, K·a = 10) and the picture barely changes: that limit is the Dirichlet process with concentration alpha = K·a. Lower a to 0.001 (K·a = 1) and a few pieces take almost everything.
Hover over the bar (or use the piece picker) to read a piece’s weight rho_k.







Components are the infinitely many atoms of the model; clusters are the ones the J units actually occupy. On this site K_J always counts clusters: the number of fitted components among the J units. After Broderick (MLSS 2016, part I, demos 3 and 4); the mathematics is re-implemented and no code is copied.



Standalone version: embed/paintbox.html, for example ?n=100 or ?K=5000&a=0.002&n=200.

title: K_J is a random variable, and five exercises
text:
The number of occupied tables K_J is not a fixed consequence of alpha: seat J customers with the same alpha in a hundred restaurants and you get a hundred different values. Their distribution is the Antoniak pmf, P(K_J = k | alpha) = |s(J, k)| alpha^k Γ(alpha) / Γ(alpha + J), which every prior statement about K_J on this site builds on.
Press 100 replicates (or Enter) a few times. The dots pile up where the bars predict, and their mean approaches E(K_J | alpha): 5.19 for J = 100 and alpha = 1. K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units.

Exercises

title: The Dirichlet process mixture, generated
text: The Dirichlet process mixture puts the pieces together. Each new point draws a uniform u. If u falls inside a piece of the stick that already exists, the point joins that piece’s cluster. If it falls in the unbroken rest, the stick is broken further, one Beta(1, alpha) proportion at a time, until a piece covers u; every new piece also gets a new mean, drawn from the base distribution N(0, sigma0^2). The point then lands near its piece’s mean, with spread sigma.

title: The Dirichlet process mixture, generated
text:
What to try

Add 1 (or Enter) a few times, then Add 100. Three counters move at different speeds: N grows by one per point, components by one per new piece of stick, clusters by one per piece that receives its first point. Clusters grow roughly like alpha log N (the dashed curve).
Look for lonely black squares. A u that lands far to the right forces several breaks at once; the pieces it skipped get means but no points. Those are components without a cluster.
Hover over a piece of the stick (or use the component picker) to light up its points and its mean.
alpha, sigma0, sigma. alpha sets how quickly new pieces are needed; sigma0 how far apart the means are; sigma how tight each cluster is.







On this site K_J counts clusters, the fitted components among the J units, not the components the process has created. After Broderick (MLSS 2016, part II, demo 6); the mathematics is re-implemented and no code is copied.



Standalone version: embed/dpmm.html, for example ?alpha=5&n=300.

title: The Chinese restaurant process
text: Imagine the J units of a study (sites, schools, studies) arriving one at a time at a restaurant with infinitely many tables. The first sits at table 1. Unit n + 1 joins an occupied table k with probability n_k / (alpha + n), where n_k is the number already there, and opens a new table with probability alpha / (alpha + n). Large tables attract more newcomers (“the rich get richer”), and alpha works like a pseudo-count for the tables nobody has sat at yet.

title: The Chinese restaurant process
text:
What to try

alpha = 1, Seat 1 eight times. The factor strip below the bar reproduces Broderick’s example: the probability of a seating is the product of one factor per arrival, alpha/alpha for the first, then n_k/(alpha + n) or alpha/(alpha + n).
Seat 100 at alpha = 0.01, then at alpha = 2. With a tiny alpha nearly everyone ends up at one table; with alpha = 2 a handful of tables share the room.
The STAR read-out. With J = 79 schools, the 79th school opens a new cluster with probability alpha/(alpha + 78): 1.3% at alpha = 1 and 6.0% at alpha = 5. By then the expected number of clusters is E(K_79 | alpha) = Σ alpha/(alpha + i − 1).
Say sites and clusters relabels the picture in the language of a multisite study.







After Broderick (MLSS 2016, Cádiz, part II; 2012 tutorial); re-implemented from the mathematics. The seating is seeded, so the same seed and alpha reproduce the same restaurant. Keyboard: Tab to the controls; Enter seats one more.



Standalone version: embed/crp.html (for example ?alpha=0.5).

title: The Chinese restaurant process
text:
How K_N grows (P-08)
Follow the number of occupied tables K_N as customers keep arriving. Its expectation E[K_N] = Σ alpha/(alpha + n − 1) grows like alpha log N: slowly, but without bound. At a fixed N, the exact distribution of K_N is the Antoniak distribution, which is exactly what the rest of the site calls the prior of K_J for a study with J = N units.



At alpha = 1 and N = 100, E[K_100] = 5.19: the average of the black curve and the mean of the bars in panel B are the same number. Add 1000 customers and switch the N axis to log: the staircase follows alpha log N. The dotted guides mark N = 48, 79 and 500, the sizes of the paper’s three applications.

title: Beta and Dirichlet: random probability vectors
text: A mixture needs weights: nonnegative numbers that add up to one. The Dirichlet distribution is a distribution over such vectors. With K = 2 it is the Beta distribution: rho_1 ~ Beta(a_1, a_2) and rho_2 = 1 − rho_1. Its parameters work like pseudo-counts: E(rho_k) = a_k / (a_1 + … + a_K), and the larger they are, the closer each draw stays to that mean.

title: Beta and Dirichlet: random probability vectors
text:
What to try

K = 2 (Beta). Press Draw again (or Enter) a few times, or switch on auto-draw. At a = 1 every value of rho_1 is equally likely. At a = 0.01 almost every draw puts nearly all weight on one of the two components. At a = 1000 both stay near one half. The right panel shows the Beta density with the current rho_1 in red.
K = 5 to 12 (Dirichlet). The same rule with more components: small a concentrates each draw on one or two components, large a flattens it towards 1/K (dashed line).
K = 3 and the ternary view. Every draw is a point in a triangle whose corners are (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1). The presets show the three shapes: a = 0.5 pushes the points into the corners, a = 5 gathers them in the centre, and a = (40, 10, 10) pulls them towards rho_1 = 40/60 = 2/3.
set each a_k gives every component its own parameter.

As K grows and a shrinks with K·a held fixed, the Dirichlet draw starts to look like the stick-breaking weights of the Dirichlet process (paintbox, stick-breaking).






After Broderick (MLSS 2016, part I, demos 1 and 2); the mathematics is re-implemented and no code is copied.

Part 1 built the Dirichlet process mixture from stick-breaking and the Chinese restaurant process. This part keeps that language and asks what a Gamma(a, b) hyperprior on the concentration parameter alpha says about clusters. Eight widgets, in the order of the argument:

2. One alpha, two lenses. The same alpha fixes how many clusters the J units occupy (the count view, K_J) and how large a random unit’s cluster is (the weight view, W_SB). Only the first depends on J. A Gamma prior on alpha mixes many conditional pmfs into one.

title: Gamma mixing: from alpha nodes to the marginal pmf
text:
Given alpha, the number of clusters K_J has the Antoniak pmf P(K_J = k | alpha) = |s(J, k)| alpha^k Γ(alpha) / Γ(alpha + J), where |s(J, k)| are unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind. With a Gamma(a, b) prior on alpha, the prior pmf of K_J averages these conditional pmfs over the prior: P(K_J = k) = ∫ P(K_J = k | alpha) Gamma(alpha; a, b) d alpha.
The widget computes the average in the plainest way. It cuts log alpha into n equal slices, puts a node at the centre of each slice, and weights that node’s pmf by the prior probability of its slice. Every thin line is one node; the thick line is the weighted sum.

title: Gamma mixing: from alpha nodes to the marginal pmf
text:
What to try

Drag the node count from 20 to 400 under Gamma(1, 1) at J = 100. With 20 nodes the sum misses the exact marginal pmf by an L1 distance of .023 and its mean is 4.90. With 400 nodes the gap is 5.0e-5 and the mean is 4.838, against the exact 4.837. Each doubling of the node count cuts the gap about fourfold (the error panel keeps the 20-node scale, so the bars shrink).
Hover over a thin line, or over a tick in the strip below it (or focus the strip and use the arrow keys). Small alpha puts almost all mass on K_J = 1; large alpha spreads it over many clusters. No single node looks like the marginal pmf.
Switch to “one alpha = E(alpha)”. Gamma(1, 1) has prior mean alpha = 1, and at alpha = 1 alone E K_100 = 5.19 with variance 3.55. Mixing over the prior gives mean 4.84 and variance 13.2: the uncertainty about alpha widens the count view.







The engine behind every widget on this site uses the same idea with a finer grid: at least 400 nodes on log alpha plus end corrections, checked against DPprior in R (pmf entries to 1e-8, moments to 1e-4). That is why a full pmf of K_J takes milliseconds.

title: The unintended prior in 1000 restaurants
text: Part 3 read the Gamma(1.60, 1.22) hyperprior of paper Figure 1 through two formulas. Here the same prior runs as a process. Each restaurant draws its own alpha from Gamma(1.60, 1.22), then seats J = 50 customers by the Chinese restaurant rule: an occupied table with probability proportional to its size, a new table with probability proportional to alpha. The widget repeats this for 1000 restaurants.

title: The unintended prior in 1000 restaurants
text:
What the restaurants say

About five tables. The table counts pile up around five; the dots are the exact prior pmf of K_50 (mean 5.05), and with seed 1 the 1000 restaurants average 5.04 tables.
One table often seats most of the room. In about 63% of the restaurants the largest table holds more than 25 of the 50 customers. The analyst asked for “about five clusters” and also got, without asking, a prior in which one cluster usually dominates.
Two probabilities, two questions. Pr(W_SB > .5) = .487 asks whether the table of a randomly chosen customer holds more than half of the population. Pr(W_max > .5) = .636 asks whether the largest table does. The second is always at least the first (Proposition 1 of the paper bounds it between S(.5) and 2 S(.5)); the red share in the simulation estimates a 50-customer version of it.

Press Simulate 1000 restaurants (or Enter) for a new seed, hover over the wall of squares to open one restaurant, or move a and b: at Gamma(1, 3) most restaurants have one or two tables and the red squares take over.






These are prior statements: no data have been seen. K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units.

title: A vocabulary test: 500 respondents, 13 words
text: The third application is psychometric. A 13-word vocabulary checklist (Open-Source Psychometrics Project, via the Item Response Warehouse) is fitted with a Rasch model whose ability distribution is a Dirichlet process mixture, for 500 respondents. The elicited statement is “about five latent groups, between 2 and 10 with 80% probability”.

title: A vocabulary test: 500 respondents, 13 words
section: The groups change, the person scores do not
text:
The groups change, the person scores do not
The same fits describe the ability distribution and score the people. Below, the fitted densities follow the priors checked above. Neither the distribution nor the 500 respondents’ scores move with the prior; only the number of groups does.




The ability distribution is the same under every prior: the fitted densities differ from the Vague one by at most .002. The stronger priors use more groups to describe the same shape. The Gaussian benchmark (grey) is flatter.
The person scores stay put: a score group’s posterior ability moves by .031 logits under the Dual-Anchor prior, and the WLE scores by at most .006. The 63 perfect scores have a WLE SE of 1.73, the widest in the sample.

Standalone versions: embed/rasch-kpmf.html (for example ?preset=count25) and embed/rasch-density.html.

title: Project STAR: 79 schools
text: Project STAR randomised pupils to small and regular classes within 79 Tennessee schools. The paper fits the Dirichlet process mixture to the 79 school-level effects under five priors on alpha. Switch the prior below: the schools hardly move.

title: Project STAR: 79 schools
section: The number of clusters does depend on the prior
text:
The number of clusters does depend on the prior
The same five priors imply very different beliefs about K_79, the number of fitted components among the 79 schools, and the data do not wash that out. The selector below follows the one above.



The prior on K_79. Vague expects 4.61 clusters (90% interval [1, 11]) with Pr(W_SB > .5) = .591; the Dual-Anchor prior (lambda = .20) expects 6.24 [3, 10] with .385; the hard bound is nearly a point mass at alpha = 2 (a above 3 million), with 7.93 and .250.
What the data leave. The posterior E(K | data) goes from 1.96 under Vague to 4.47 under the Dual-Anchor prior, and the chance of a single cluster for all 79 schools from .560 to .064. The largest observed share falls from .920 to .724. These posterior numbers come from the replication package; only the prior side is computed here.

Standalone versions: embed/star-caterpillar.html and embed/app-prior-strip.html (for example ?preset=da).

title: The partition moves, the effects do not
text: The same data, three priors on alpha. The top row is what the prior is about (the partition: how many clusters, how large the largest one is); the bottom row is what most analyses report (the unit effects).

title: The partition moves, the effects do not
text:
The specification matters too




Wide scale. With the grand-mean prior N(0, 100) and the matching scale, the Dual-Anchor fit to STAR drops from 4.47 to 2.85 clusters and its collapse probability rises from .064 to .318.
The HC3 input. Replacing the multilevel school estimates by schoolwise OLS/HC3 ones moves the school posterior means by RMS .169 to .174, about 20 times the difference between priors, and 22 of 79 intervals then exclude zero. This is a specification sensitivity, not a robustness check: the structural summaries move with the model and its uncertainty input, not only with the concentration prior.

title: Released data behind the evidence pages
text:
The evidence pages read summary tables that the replication package (joonho112/DPprior-paper-replication) releases. They are copied, not recomputed: no MCMC runs in the browser, and no pupil-level, response-level or individual posterior-draw data are included. A contract file records each table’s source, level, rows, columns, sha256 and licence scope, and the site’s verification gate (verification/check_data_contract.mjs) fails if a table changes, loses or gains a column, contains an individual-level field, or lacks its rights statement.
What CC BY 4.0 covers. The grant covers the author’s contribution and nothing more. The simulation and calibration tables are the author’s own output and are covered whole. The application tables hold the author’s posterior summaries of data that belong to others, and the per-unit inputs in star_units.json and bd_units.json (the estimate tau_hat, its standard error se and the size n_j) come straight from those data: Project STAR through the R package mlmRev, and Bangert-Drowns, Hurley and Wilkinson (2004) through the R package metadat. Both packages are distributed under GPL (>= 2), a package licence rather than a separate grant for the original study data, so these inputs keep their upstream terms and are not relicensed here. The vocabulary tables derive from an Item Response Warehouse table whose derived licence is CC BY 4.0, subject to upstream rights (collected by the Open-Source Psychometrics Project; scale by Brotherton, French and Pickering, 2013). Each card below states its table’s scope, upstream source and terms, following the replication package’s LICENSE-SCOPE.md and provenance/data-rights.csv.
One table is the declared exception: rasch_respondents.json holds anonymous derived values for the 500 respondents of the vocabulary application (row number, raw score, WLE, its SE and a perfect-score flag), re-derived from the public Item Response Warehouse table with the replication package’s sampling rule and scoring code. text:
Instructor notes

Offline. Every widget is a small script bundled with the site, so the pages and the standalone versions also work from a downloaded copy of the site (file://) with no network. The videos and the static fallbacks need no JavaScript at all.
The same draws for everyone. Widgets with random draws take a seed (?seed=1 in the links above), so a class sees the same sticks, tables and points.
Three confusions to name early. Components against clusters (K_J counts the occupied ones); the size-biased weight W_SB against the largest weight W_max (the first is a lower bound for the second when t ≥ 1/2); prior collapse Pr(K_J = 1) against posterior collapse Pr(K_J = 1 | data). The vocabulary page has the site’s terms.
Timing. The course route fits one 90-minute session with the exercises as an in-class break; the beginner route works as the first half hour of a workshop, the researcher route as a lab after a talk on the paper.
After the session. The catalog lists all 72 visualizations with what each one shows; the released data page lists the tables the evidence pages read.

title: DPprior Explorer
text: This site is a pool of interactive visualizations built around Design-Conditional Prior Elicitation for Dirichlet Process Mixtures (Lee, 2026, arXiv:2602.06301). It assumes no prior knowledge of Dirichlet process mixtures (DPMs). Its numbers come by two routes. Prior quantities for any Gamma(a, b) or fixed alpha (cluster counts, weight tails, calibrations, the default-method solvers) are computed in your browser by one JavaScript engine, which is compared with the DPprior R package (version 2.0.0) and with independent R integrals. Posterior, simulation and application results are read from released summary tables of the replication package and never recomputed. How the numbers are checked says what each check covers.

title: DPprior Explorer
text:
The storyline

Learn the DPM. Following Broderick’s MLSS 2016 ladder: why a nonparametric prior, Beta and Dirichlet weights, many components and few clusters, stick-breaking (GEM), the Chinese restaurant process, and the DP mixture.
The CRP bridge. One concentration parameter alpha sets both how many tables open among J units (the count view, K_J) and how large the tables are (the weight view, W_SB). A Gamma(a, b) hyperprior on alpha is read in the same table-and-stick language.
What default hyperpriors imply. A “vague” default says different things at different J (same default, different J); a prior calibrated to “about five clusters” can still put a random unit in a majority cluster with probability .49 (the unintended prior).
The DPprior principle. State a design-conditional target, calibrate Gamma(a, b) to it (TSMM), diagnose the implied weights, and decide whether a Dual-Anchor adjustment is needed.
Evidence. Simulation and three applications: STAR (J = 79 schools), Bangert-Drowns (J = 48 studies) and a vocabulary checklist (N = 500 respondents), drawn only from released summaries.

Terms are defined on the vocabulary page.

    P-00 Step 6.1 · done
    Why nonparametric Bayes?
    A finite mixture fixes its number of cells before seeing data, while a Dirichlet process keeps unbroken stick mass for cells nobody has used yet, so the number of occupied cells can grow with N.
    You do: The viewer switches between K = 2, K = 5 and K = infinity, moves N from 10 to 500, and presses Redraw (or Enter) for new weights, centres and points.
    You see: A two-dimensional scatter coloured by cell with the occupied cell centres marked, and a bar of the cell weights above the shares of the N points, with a dashed 'new cells' piece of unbroken stick when K is infinite.
    dp-core sampler (seeded Dirichlet, Beta(1, alpha), normal) + Observable Plot 0.6.17
    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-01 Step 6.2 · done
    Beta lollipop
    rho_1 ~ Beta(a_1, a_2) with rho_2 = 1 - rho_1 is the two-component case of the Dirichlet: small a gives nearly all-or-nothing draws and large a nearly even ones.
    You do: The viewer moves the shared a on a log slider from 0.01 to 1000 or sets a_1 and a_2 separately, presses Draw again (or Enter), and switches on auto-draw at two draws per second and the twenty ghosts.
    You see: Two lollipop stems for rho_1 and rho_2 with the previous twenty draws as faint dots, and the Beta(a_1, a_2) density of rho_1 with the current draw marked in red.
    dp-core sampler (seeded, log-scale Dirichlet) + Observable Plot 0.6.17
    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-02 Step 6.2 · done
    Dirichlet lollipop and ternary view
    rho ~ Dirichlet(a_1, ..., a_K) spreads a draw evenly when a is large and concentrates it on few components when a is small; at K = 3 each draw is a point in a triangle.
    You do: The viewer sets K from 2 to 12 and a (shared or per component), draws again or auto-draws, and at K = 3 picks the presets a = 0.5, a = 5 and a = (40, 10, 10).
    You see: K lollipop stems with ghosts and a 1/K reference line and, at K = 3, 300 draws in the triangle that gather in the corners (a = 0.5), in the centre (a = 5) or towards rho_1 = 2/3 (a = (40, 10, 10)).
    dp-core sampler (seeded, log-scale Dirichlet) + Observable Plot 0.6.17
    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-03 Step 6.3 · done
    Large-K paintbox with falling markers
    A Dirichlet(a, ..., a) draw with K = 1000 and a = 0.01 cuts the unit interval into a few wide pieces and many slivers; uniform drops occupy far fewer pieces (clusters) than there are components.
    You do: The viewer presses Drop 1, Drop 10 or Drop 100 and New rho, moves a from 0.001 to 1 and K from 100 to 5000, and hovers over the bar or uses the piece picker.
    You see: The unit-interval bar with hit pieces turning from grey to blue as red markers fall, the number of drops and of occupied pieces against the exact expectation (24.2 after 100 drops at K = 1000, a = 0.01), the equivalent alpha = K a, and one piece's rho_k.

    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-04 Step 6.3 · done
    Order-of-appearance staircase
    Numbering clusters in the order they are first hit gives a concave staircase: new clusters appear ever more rarely, roughly like alpha log N with alpha = K a.
    You do: The viewer drops points in the linked paintbox and switches the drop-number axis between linear and log scales.
    You see: Every drop plotted at (drop number, cluster by order of appearance), first hits in blue joined by a step frontier, with component and cluster counters in step with the paintbox.

    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-05 Step 4.1 · done
    GEM stick-breaking staircase
    With V_k ~ Beta(1, alpha) and w_k = V_k times what is left, a small alpha lets the first piece take most of the stick (E[w_1] = 1/(1 + alpha), Pr(w_1 > .5) = 0.5^alpha).
    You do: The viewer moves the alpha slider or picks the presets 0.5, 1, 2, 10 and 100, presses Break again (Enter) or Step, switches between size-biased and ranked order, and turns on 20 ghost rows.

    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-06 Step 6.4 · done
    Hoppe urn to stick-breaking
    Hoppe's urn with one black ball of mass alpha is the Chinese restaurant process; its colour shares converge to one draw of stick-breaking weights, so the first colour's long-run share is W_1 ~ Beta(1, alpha).
    You do: The viewer sets alpha, draws one ball at a time (Step or Enter), adds 10 or 100, plays automatically at three speeds, resets, and runs the 1000-urn experiment.
    You see: The urn with its black alpha ball and coloured balls, a strip of the first four draws with their probabilities, the colour-share bar and the first colour's share settling over draws, and a histogram of 1000 first-colour shares on the Beta(1, alpha) density.
    dp-core CRP sampler (seeded) + D3 7.9.0 + Observable Plot 0.6.17
    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-07 Step 4.2 · done
    Chinese restaurant process
    Customer n + 1 joins table k with probability n_k/(alpha + n) and a new table with probability alpha/(alpha + n): alpha is a pseudo-count for the tables not seen yet.
    You do: The viewer sets alpha (presets 0.01, 0.5, 1, 2), seats 1, 10 or 100 customers, plays or pauses at three speeds, resets, changes the seed, and switches the labels to sites and clusters.

    P-08 Step 4.4 · done
    How K_N grows
    E[K_N] = sum alpha/(alpha + n - 1), about alpha log N, and the distribution of K_N at the current N is the Antoniak pmf, which is the prior of K_J for J = N.
    You do: The viewer sets alpha, adds 1, 10, 100 or 1000 customers, switches the N axis between linear and log, and turns 20 ghost paths on or off.

    DP mixture generator (N, components, clusters)
    Generating a Dirichlet process mixture by lazy stick-breaking creates pieces and means only when a point needs them, so points, components created and clusters grow at different speeds and some components stay empty.
    You do: The viewer sets alpha (default 2), sigma0 (1.5) and sigma (0.3), adds 1, 10 or 100 points (Enter adds one), resets, and hovers over a piece of the stick or uses the component picker.

    page · standalone
  


  
  
    P-10 Step 6.6 · done
    Distributions ladder (Beta, Dirichlet, GEM, DP atoms)
    One concentration alpha drives Beta, Dirichlet, GEM and Dirichlet process draws whose support grows from two points to K points, to the positive integers, to the real line.
    You do: The viewer moves the shared alpha, draws each row separately (or new atom locations for row 4), and presses Redraw all (or Enter).

    P-11 Step 6.7 · done
    A draw G from the Dirichlet process
    A Dirichlet process draw G = sum_k w_k delta(phi_k) combines GEM(alpha) weights with locations from the base distribution, so it is discrete and draws from it repeat.
    You do: The viewer sets alpha and the spread sigma0 of the base distribution, presses New G (or Enter), sets N and presses Sample N points.

    DP or not: finite versus GEM
    A finite Dirichlet mixture uses at most K components however large N gets, while stick-breaking weights keep supplying new components, so K_N grows like alpha log N; with a_k = alpha/K a large-K mixture imitates the Dirichlet process for a long time but still cannot pass K.

    Collapsed Gibbs CRP sampler
    Collapsed Gibbs sampling for a DP mixture resamples each point's cluster with probability proportional to the CRP prior weight times the fit, and alpha = 0.01 is a strong prior against new clusters.

title: Bangert-Drowns: 48 writing-to-learn studies
text:
The second application is a meta-analysis: 48 studies of writing-to-learn interventions (Bangert-Drowns, Hurley, and Wilkinson, 2004). The same Dirichlet process mixture treats the study effects as draws from an unknown distribution of effects. The paper’s target for the number of clusters is “about 4, between 1 and 8 with 80% probability”.






The same pattern as STAR. From Vague to the Dual-Anchor prior the posterior number of clusters goes from 1.89 to 3.31, and the chance that all 48 studies share one cluster from .548 to .190, while the study effects move by less than .01 in root mean square and the same 13 posterior intervals exclude zero.
A classical benchmark. The random-effects estimate (REML) from the reported effects is .222 with a 95% interval [.132, .312] and I² = 58.4%: a heterogeneous literature, which is why the number of clusters is worth a prior at all.
Moderators. The slopes of the study effects on grade and on length hardly change with the prior (a descriptive alignment, not causal moderation).







Study-level effects and standard errors: metadat::dat.bangertdrowns2004 (metadat 1.6-0, GPL ≥ 2), as used by the replication package; posterior summaries and moderator slopes: the replication package (CC BY 4.0). The random-effects benchmark is computed in the browser from the released effects and standard errors; it is not a posterior quantity.



Standalone version: embed/bd-forest.html (for example ?preset=da or ?preset=moderators).

title: Part 5 · Evidence and real data
text:
Default concentration hyperpriors can strongly shape conclusions about heterogeneity; our design-conditional framework makes those choices explicit by calibrating the prior to an expected cluster count and checking its implied cluster sizes.

The pages below show that statement in released results. In every application the prior moves the partition (the number of clusters, the chance of a single cluster, the largest weight) while the unit effects stay put (A-11), and the model specification can matter as much as the prior (A-12). Simulation results and three applications (STAR, J = 79 schools; Bangert-Drowns, J = 48 studies; a vocabulary checklist, N = 500), drawn only from released summaries.

title: The simulation: what the prior moves and what it does not
text: The paper simulates multisite trials with J = 100 sites, a generating number of components K* of 5, 10 or 30, and three levels of information I (how much each site’s data say about its own effect). Each cell is fitted 200 times under five priors on alpha.

title: The simulation: what the prior moves and what it does not
section: The effects stay, the partition moves
text:
The effects stay, the partition moves




Fixed lambda. Holding the Dual-Anchor lambda at .16 (the selected value), .5 or .9 moves the posterior number of clusters from 2.47 to 1.76 to 1.54, and the RMSE by less than .001.
Unequal weights. With one cluster holding 60% of the sites the pattern is the same: the RMSE is flat across priors, the collapse rate is not.

title: The simulation: what the prior moves and what it does not
section: When the elicited mean is wrong
text:
When the elicited mean is wrong
The paper’s misspecification grid states the target mean as r = mu_K / K* times the truth, with r = .5, 1 or 2 (medium confidence, J = 100, grand-mean prior N(0, 100)).




The posterior follows the elicited mean. Under TSMM at K* = 10 and I = .2 the posterior mean of K_J moves from 1.51 to 3.41 to 15.03 as mu_K goes from 5 to 10 to 20.
Same mean, same answer. The cells (K* = 5, r = 2) and (K* = 10, r = 1) share mu_K = 10 and both give 3.41, with collapse .391 in both, although the true counts differ by a factor of two. Switch the horizontal axis to mu_K and the trajectories for different K* fall on one curve.
The weight anchor matters only at small mu_K. At mu_K = 5 (K* = 10, r = .5) Dual-Anchor raises the posterior mean from 1.51 to 2.48; from mu_K = 10 on, the trigger does not fire and Dual-Anchor coincides with TSMM.

title: The simulation: what the prior moves and what it does not
section: More sites do not fix the default
text:
More sites do not fix the default
The design-size grid runs the same priors at J = 25, 50, 100 and 200 sites (K* = 5 or 10, I = .2 or .8, grand-mean prior N(0, 100)).




The default stays collapsed. Under Vague the posterior mean of K_J stays between 1.18 and 1.46 and the collapse probability is at least .765 even at J = 200.
Dual-Anchor moves toward the reference count. At K* = 5 and I = .2 its posterior mean goes from 1.53 at J = 25 to 3.50 at J = 200 (collapse .716 to .271) while TSMM stays near 1.5; the selected lambda changes from .70 to .30, .16 and .09 along the way, so this is a policy trajectory, not a sample-size effect alone.
SSI-Weight ignores the design. Its trajectories are the same at K* = 5 and K* = 10 (2.17 to 2.99 and 2.16 to 2.99 at I = .2), with collapse near .5.
At I = .8 and J = 200 only 30 to 93 of 200 fits pass the diagnostics; those points are hollow.

title: Collapse: everyone at the first table
text: In the restaurant, customer n + 1 opens a new table with probability alpha / (alpha + n). When alpha is close to 0 that almost never happens, and every customer ends up at the first table: P(K_J = 1 | alpha) = ∏ i / (i + alpha) over i = 1, …, J − 1, which is .906 for J = 79 and alpha = 0.02. A Gamma(a, b) prior on alpha keeps some mass near 0, so it assigns a prior probability to this collapse: all J units in one cluster.

title: Collapse: everyone at the first table
text:
Reading the panels

A. Mass near 0. Gamma(1, 1) puts Pr(alpha < .1) = .095 below alpha = .1. The TSMM prior for “about five clusters” at J = 100 with the widest confidence setting (VIF 5, paper Table 2) puts .182 there: a vaguer statement about the number of clusters buys more mass near alpha = 0.
B. Prior collapse. Under Gamma(1, 1), P(K_J = 1) is .192 at J = 50, .175 at J = 79, .168 at J = 100 and .132 at J = 500. Under the VIF 5 prior it is .262, .247, .240 and .204.
C. The restaurant at small alpha. Press Play (or Enter): at alpha = 0.02 all 79 customers usually share one table. Switch the restaurant alpha to 0.1 or 1 and play again.







Prior versus posterior collapse. P(K_J = 1) is a prior statement, made before any data. Pr(K_J = 1 | data) is a posterior statement about a fitted model. For STAR (79 schools) under Gamma(1, 1) the prior value is .175 and the released posterior value is .560; the widget reads the posterior value from the replication package and does not recompute it. K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units.

title: Dominance in stick-breaking rows
text: Stick-breaking builds the cluster weights one piece at a time: V_k ~ Beta(1, alpha) and w_k = V_k × (what is left of the stick). The first piece has a special reading. It is the size-biased weight W_SB: the population share of the cluster that a randomly chosen unit belongs to. Its tail has a closed form under a Gamma(a, b) hyperprior, S(t) = Pr(W_SB > t) = (b / (b − log(1 − t)))^a.

title: Dominance in stick-breaking rows
section: M-17 · How often does the first piece take more than half?
text:
M-17 · How often does the first piece take more than half?
Each row below draws its own alpha from the hyperprior and then breaks one stick. The first piece is in colour; a red dot marks the rows where it passes one half. Press Redraw (or Enter) a few times: the running share settles near S(.5).






Gamma(1, 1): S(.5) = .591. More than half of the rows have a first piece above one half.
Gamma(1, 3): S(.5) = .812. The hyperprior puts more mass near alpha = 0, and most sticks break almost whole at the first cut.
Dual-Anchor Gamma(2.32, 1.42): S(.5) = .398. This is the J = 50 worked example’s Dual-Anchor prior (Part 4), which keeps “about five clusters” while bringing S(.5) under its .40 trigger.

title: Dominance in stick-breaking rows
section: M-18 · The first piece is not always the largest
text:
M-18 · The first piece is not always the largest
The same draws again, each row shown twice: in breaking order (top) and sorted by size (bottom). A red dot marks rows where the first piece to break off is not the largest.


When the first piece is above one half, the other pieces share less than one half, so the first piece is the largest. The reverse fails: the largest piece can break off later. That is why Pr(W_SB > .5) is a lower bound for Pr(W_max > .5), the probability that the largest cluster holds more than half of the population.

title: Dominance in stick-breaking rows
section: C-16 · How far apart can W_SB and W_max be?
text:
C-16 · How far apart can W_SB and W_max be?
Proposition 1 of the paper turns the M-18 argument into a band. For t of one half or more,
S(t) ≤ Pr(W_max > t) ≤ min(1, S(t) / t),
and the engine also computes the middle term exactly (a one-dimensional integral after the substitution u = −log(1 − w)). Under Gamma(1, 1) at t = .5 the band is [.591, 1] and the exact value is .728. As t grows the two tails meet: a random unit falls in a piece larger than t with probability at least t, so at t = .9 the tails are .303 (W_SB) and .309 (W_max).



The STAR posterior switch adds the application’s released posterior summaries (paper Table 5) for the five STAR priors. They are posterior quantities, conditional on the 79 schools, and are read from the replication package, not recomputed. Under the vague Gamma(1, 1) prior the largest occupied cluster holds .920 of the schools on average and the posterior probability that the largest population weight exceeds one half is .963; under the Dual-Anchor prior these drop to .724 and .804, and the alpha-only size-biased probability drops from .797 to .419.






W_SB is the share of a random unit’s cluster, never “the largest weight”. Size-biased dominance and W_max are named separately throughout this site. These are prior statements. Stick-breaking rows after Broderick (MLSS 2016; 2012 tutorial), with the mathematics re-implemented.

title: What Gamma(1, 1) actually says
text: Gamma(1, 1) is the usual “vague” default for the concentration parameter. It is vague about alpha: the prior spreads alpha over two orders of magnitude. It is not vague about clusters. Read through the Chinese restaurant process and stick-breaking, the same prior makes definite statements about how many clusters there are, how large the cluster of a random unit is, and how likely it is that everyone shares one cluster.

title: What Gamma(1, 1) actually says
text:
Five readings at J = 100

alpha. Pr(alpha ≤ .5) = .393: two in five draws of alpha are small enough that a new table is rarely opened.
Number of clusters. E K_100 = 4.84 with a 90% interval of [1, 12]. Change J and this tile moves: 2.65 at J = 10, 6.44 at J = 500, 8.73 at J = 5000 (for J above 500 the band is precomputed in R).
Size of a random unit’s cluster. Pr(W_SB > .5) = .591 and Pr(W_SB > .9) = .303, at every J.
Seventy-nine sites, twenty times. Simulated sets of 79 sites (the STAR schools) show the typical pattern: one large cluster and a few small ones, and now and then a single cluster for all 79.
Prior collapse. P(K_100 = 1) = .168: before any data, the prior gives about one chance in six that all 100 units form a single cluster.

The literature presets move all five tiles at once. Gamma(1, 3) puts more mass near alpha = 0: Pr(W_SB > .5) = .812. Gamma(0.037, 0.037), the SCAL shortcut of Part 3, is vaguer still about alpha and gives P(K_100 = 1) = .834.






Vague in alpha is not vague in clusters. A flat-looking prior on the concentration parameter is a strong prior on the partition. The value .834 for Gamma(0.037, 0.037) at J = 100 comes from an adaptive integral in R and from this page’s engine; an earlier .824 came from a coarse 80-node quadrature and is not used. These are prior statements. K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units.

title: One alpha, two lenses
text: A Dirichlet process mixture has one concentration parameter, alpha. In the Chinese restaurant process it is a pseudo-count for tables nobody has opened yet: customer n + 1 opens a new table with probability alpha / (alpha + n) (see the restaurant). The same alpha answers two different questions about the prior.

title: One alpha, two lenses
text:
What to try

Start at Gamma(1, 1), J = 100. The count view has mean 4.84 and variance 13.2, with a 90% interval of [1, 12]. The weight view gives Pr(W_SB > .5) = .591, Pr(W_SB > .9) = .303 and E(rho) = .596.
Move J from 10 to 500. E K_J climbs from 2.65 to 6.44. The weight view and the gauge do not move: Pr(W_SB > t) = (b / (b − log(1 − t)))^a involves only a and b.
Try Gamma(1, 3). More prior mass near alpha = 0 means fewer clusters (E K_100 = 2.50) and a bigger cluster for a random unit (Pr(W_SB > .5) = .812). The two views move together because they share alpha.
Switch to a fixed alpha and drag it from 0.01 to 100. At alpha = 1, E K_100 = 5.19 with variance 3.55: without a prior on alpha the count view is much narrower.







Elicitation of “about five clusters” targets the count view. Size-biased dominance, Pr(W_SB > t), lives in the weight view. A hyperprior calibrated only on the count view still decides the weight view, which is the unintended prior of Part 3. These are prior statements.

title: A collapsed Gibbs sampler for the CRP mixture
text:
The last rung runs the model backwards: given the data, which clusters? The collapsed Gibbs sampler (Neal’s Algorithm 3) visits one point at a time. It takes the point out of its cluster and puts it back with probability proportional to
where n_c is the number of other points in cluster c. The first factor is the Chinese restaurant prior; the second is the likelihood with the cluster centre integrated out.

title: A collapsed Gibbs sampler for the CRP mixture
text:
What to try

Step point (or Enter) a few times and compare the two bars: the CRP prior weight says “join a big cluster”; the posterior multiplies in how well the point fits each cluster. The dashed piece is a new cluster.
Start from one cluster, singletons or a random split. From one cluster the sampler splits off the four true clusters within a sweep or two; from 100 singletons or a random split it merges them over ten to twenty sweeps, because single points move one at a time.
alpha. The demo in Broderick’s tutorial fixes alpha = 0.01, so a new cluster starts with one hundredth of the weight of a one-point cluster. That is a strong prior. Move alpha to 1 or 10 while playing: the sampler keeps more small clusters, and the level of K in the trace moves up.
true means overlays the four centres the data came from.







The number of clusters here, K after a sweep, is a draw from the posterior of K_J for J = 100 units, not a prior statement. The sampler holds sigma = 1 and a N(0, 3²) prior on cluster centres fixed. text: Every rung so far has drawn a random distribution: a set of weights on some set of points. The four rows below use one concentration alpha and differ only in what the weights sit on.

title: Distributions and Dirichlet process atoms
text:
Reading the rows

Beta(alpha/2, alpha/2) puts weight on two points.
Dirichlet(alpha/10, …, alpha/10) puts weight on ten points. With the total alpha fixed, spreading it over more components makes each draw more uneven.
GEM(alpha), the stick-breaking weights, puts weight on 1, 2, 3, … without end; the “…” is the mass left after thirty pieces.
The Dirichlet process DP(alpha, N(0, 1)) takes the same weights and gives each one a random location phi_k drawn from the base distribution N(0, 1) (shaded). Press Redraw all (or Enter) and watch the bars of row 3 move to their locations.

Row 4 is a draw G = Σ w_k δ_{phi_k} from the Dirichlet process: a discrete distribution on the real line, with infinitely many atoms and most of its mass on a few of them.

P-11 · One draw G, three views

Because G is discrete, the samples land exactly on atoms and repeat: N = 100 draws with alpha = 2 take only a handful of distinct values (E(K_N | alpha) = 8.40). title: Distributions and Dirichlet process atoms
section: P-12 · Why choose the Dirichlet process?
text:
P-12 · Why choose the Dirichlet process?
The same widget, switched to its comparison view, sets one stick-breaking draw against two finite mixtures, with K = 5 and K = 50 components and flat Dirichlet(1, …, 1) weights. Watch K_N, the number of components that N draws actually use:


A finite mixture can never use more than its K components, so its K_N flattens at 5 or 50. The Dirichlet process keeps supplying new components, and K_N keeps growing like alpha log N. Broderick’s advice is to choose the Dirichlet process for this growth behaviour: new data may reveal new clusters. Switch the finite weights to alpha/K (same total mass) and the K = 50 mixture imitates the Dirichlet process for a very long time (this is the usual finite approximation of the DP), yet it too can never pass 50.

title: The EPPF: why the order of arrival does not matter
text:
Seat eight customers by the Chinese restaurant rule and end with the tables {1, 2, 7, 8}, {3, 5, 6} and {4}. The probability of that seating is a product of one factor per customer: alpha/(alpha + n − 1) when customer n opens a table, m/(alpha + n − 1) when it joins a table of m. The numerators collect alpha once per table and (|C| − 1)! for each table C; the denominators are the same in any order. So the product is the exchangeable partition probability function
P(Π_N) = alpha^K ∏C (|C| − 1)! / ∏{n = 1}^{N} (alpha + n − 1),
which depends only on the table sizes.

title: The EPPF: why the order of arrival does not matter
text:
What to try

Shuffle arrival order (or Enter). The factors under the customers change; the product does not. At alpha = 1 it is 1/3360 = .000298 in every order.
alpha. All orders still agree, now at a different value.
New seating draws another partition of eight customers from the restaurant; Broderick’s example brings back {1, 2, 7, 8}, {3, 5, 6}, {4}.
The exercise below the panel asks for E[K_8], the expected number of tables, and checks the answer with the engine.

Exchangeability is what lets a multisite analysis treat the units’ labels as arbitrary: only the sizes of the clusters carry information about alpha. The same product, summed over all partitions with K tables, gives the prior pmf of K_J used everywhere on this site.

title: Stick-breaking
text: Take a stick of length one. Break off a random proportion V_1 of it: that piece is the first weight, w_1 = V_1. Break off a proportion V_2 of what is left: w_2 = V_2 (1 − V_1). Keep going. With every V_k drawn from Beta(1, alpha), the weights (w_1, w_2, …) follow the GEM(alpha) distribution, the weights of a Dirichlet process.

title: Stick-breaking
text:
What to try

alpha = 0.5. The first break usually takes most of the stick: E[w_1] = 1/(1 + alpha) = .667 and Pr(w_1 > .5) = 0.5^alpha = .707.
alpha = 2, then 10. The pieces get smaller and more numerous; at alpha = 10 no single piece dominates (E[w_1] = .091, Pr(w_1 > .5) = .001).
alpha = 100. Hundreds of slivers; the stick behaves almost like a continuum.
Step reveals the staircase one break at a time, so you can read each V_k.
Ranked by size reorders the same pieces from largest to smallest.
x20 rows draws twenty more sticks with the same alpha: the spread across rows is the uncertainty that a single draw hides.

The first piece matters for everything that follows on this site: it has the same distribution as the population share of the cluster that a randomly chosen unit belongs to (the size-biased weight W_SB). That is why Pr(W_SB > .5) is the paper’s measure of majority-mass dominance.






After Broderick (MLSS 2016, Cádiz, part I; 2012 tutorial). The widget re-implements the mathematics; no code from her R demonstrations is used. Keyboard: Tab to the controls, arrow keys move the slider, Enter draws again.

title: Why nonparametric Bayes?
text:
The units in a multisite study, the respondents of a test, the studies of a meta-analysis: we usually treat them as exchangeable, so their order carries no information. De Finetti’s theorem then says the data behave as if drawn from a common distribution that is itself unknown. A convenient way to put a prior on that unknown distribution is a mixture: each unit belongs to one of several cells (clusters), and each cell has its own centre.
The question is how many cells. A finite mixture answers it before any data arrive: K = 2, say, with weights rho_1 and rho_2 = 1 − rho_1. The widget draws such a mixture in two dimensions: the weights from a Dirichlet distribution, the cell centres around the origin, the points around their centres.

title: Why nonparametric Bayes?
text:
What to try

K = 2, then K = 5. Move N from 10 to 500. The points spread over the fixed cells and the bottom bar approaches the weights on top, but no point can ever start a sixth cell.
K = ∞. Now the weights come from breaking a stick (the Dirichlet process with alpha = 1). The dashed piece is the part of the stick not yet broken. A point that lands there opens a new cell, so the number of occupied cells keeps growing with N, slowly.
Redraw (or Enter) draws new weights, centres and points.

The rest of this ladder builds the K = ∞ case step by step: the Beta and Dirichlet distributions for the weights, the paintbox and stick-breaking constructions, the urn and the Chinese restaurant process for the cells, and the Dirichlet process mixture itself.






After Broderick (MLSS 2016, part I; 2012 tutorial); the mathematics is re-implemented and no code is copied. In the rest of the site, K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied cells) among the J units.

title: Reporting the prior
text:
A calibrated hyperprior is only as useful as its report. The paper asks for eight items, fixed before any posterior simulation. Fill in the form, or press “Fill in the J = 50 example”, and copy the paragraph. The weight diagnostics and the trigger decision are computed for you from J and (a, b).






J, and why it is treated as fixed.
The elicited statement about K_J, the route used to convert it, and the resulting (mu_K, sigma^2) with a substantive justification (the elicitation form).
The calibrated (a, b), shape and rate, and the software version (the calibrator).
The prior median and central interval of K_J.
Pr(W_SB > .5) and Pr(W_SB > .9), the result for the largest weight, and E(rho).
If the .40 trigger fires, the Dual-Anchor details: soft target, the full lambda grid and the selection rule, the selected lambda, the change in the moments, and the software’s status fields (the frontier).
The hard-bound result, reported separately, including whether it is nearly a point mass.
At least one posterior sensitivity variant.

The six steps behind these items are on the workflow page.






The generated paragraph is a starting point written by this site, not text from the paper. It ends with a one-line summary, such as “J=50, Gamma(2.3158,1.4204), S(.5)=.398, lambda=.30”, for a table of priors.

title: From what you expect to a prior
text:
Say what you expect about K_J, the number of clusters among your J units, in the way that comes most naturally: an interval you would bet on with some probability, a confidence level, or a coefficient of variation. The form turns the statement into a mean and a variance for K_J, solves the Gamma(a, b) hyperprior with the same exact moments (TSMM), and checks the weights that prior implies.






An interval. “Between k_L and k_U with probability q” is read through a normal proxy: sigma_K = (k_U − k_L) / (2z), with z = 1.2816 at 80% and 1.96 at 95%. The mean is the value you give (“about 5”), or the midpoint.
STAR (J = 79): “about 5 clusters, between 2 and 8 with 80% probability” asks for sigma^2 = 5.48 and gives Gamma(5.134, 4.939). Its Pr(W_SB > .5) is .510, above .40, so the dominance trigger fires. The Bangert-Drowns (J = 48) and Vocabulary (J = 500) statements trigger too.
When the statement is too sure. At J = 100, “[3, 10] with 80% probability” asks for sigma^2 = 7.46 and gives Gamma(6.82, 4.82), with Pr(W_SB > .5) = .4002, just above the .40 trigger, and Pr(W_SB > .9) = .070. The same interval at 95% asks for sigma^2 = 3.19, below 4.52, the smallest variance any Gamma prior with mean 6.5 can give. The form says “no solution” and names the largest probability that would work.
A confidence level or a CV skips the interval: high, medium and low confidence mean VIF 1.5, 2.5 and 5 in sigma^2 = VIF (mu_K − 1), and a CV gives sigma^2 = (CV_K mu_K)^2.

When the trigger fires, the paper’s next step is the Dual-Anchor refinement, which gives up a little of the count target for less dominance: see the J = 50 worked example. To set (mu_K, sigma^2) directly, use the calibrator.
