title: Stage 1, then Stage 2: how TSMM finds Gamma(a, b)
text:
TSMM solves for Gamma(a, b) in two stages. Stage 1 (A1) pretends that K_J − 1 is negative binomial, which gives a closed-form start: for J = 50 and the target (5, 10), Gamma(2.667, 2.608). Under the exact Gamma mixture that start gives E K_50 = 4.415 and Var K_50 = 5.618, so it misses by (−0.59, −4.38). Stage 2 runs Newton on (log a, log b) with the exact moments and their derivatives, and lands on Gamma(1.4082, 1.0770) in five steps.






The start is close in shape, not in moments. The gold proxy has mean 5 and variance 10 by construction; the exact pmf at the start is narrower (variance 5.618). The first Newton step overshoots to Gamma(0.841, 0.627), with variance 13.5, and the next three close in.
The residual falls quadratically. |F| goes 4.42, 3.55, 0.41, 0.009, 5e-6 and then about 1e-11, the signature of Newton near a root.
R and the browser take the same steps. The R path (DPprior 2.0.0) and the dp-core path agree to four decimals at every step; both stop below 1e-8.

The same solver runs live in the calibrator, and all ten calibration targets are checked against R on the parity page.

title: Two anchors, one prior
text:
The Dual-Anchor refinement changes one Gamma prior, and every view of the model moves with it. Press the button to go from TSMM, which anchors the count only, to the paper’s Dual-Anchor choice at lambda = .30, which also anchors the weights.






The count gives a little. E K_50 moves from the target 5.00 to 5.88: about one more expected cluster.
The weights give a lot. Pr(W_SB > .5) falls from .497 to .398, just under the .40 trigger; the chance that two random units share a cluster falls from .518 to .439.
What changed in alpha. Its mean rises from 1.31 to 1.63 and its spread shrinks (CV .84 to .66). In restaurant terms, a newcomer is a little more willing to open a new table, so the first table dominates less often.

Use the a and b sliders to see how sensitive each view is near the Dual-Anchor choice. The full lambda frontier is on the Dual-Anchor page, and the whole workflow is on the J = 50 worked example.

title: Why the exact computation is cheap
text: Every number on this site is computed in your browser, exactly, while you move a slider. Three facts make that possible.

title: Why the exact computation is cheap
section: 1. Given alpha, the number of clusters is a sum of coin flips
text:
1. Given alpha, the number of clusters is a sum of coin flips
In the Chinese restaurant process, unit i opens a new table with probability p_i = alpha / (alpha + i − 1), independently of the other units. So K_J = B_1 + … + B_J with B_i ~ Bernoulli(p_i). Its mean and variance are sums, and its pmf is a convolution that takes J² steps. At alpha = 1 and J = 500 the convolution lands on the Antoniak pmf from Stirling numbers to within 1e-10, and E K_500 = H_500 = 6.79.

title: Why the exact computation is cheap
section: 2. Over alpha, the prior is a finite mixture
text:
2. Over alpha, the prior is a finite mixture
A Gamma prior on alpha mixes these pmfs. On a quadrature grid of alpha nodes the mixture is a weighted sum, and a few hundred nodes are enough: below, the J = 50 TSMM prior Gamma(1.4082, 1.0770) starts at 20 nodes; drag the node count up and watch the error vanish.

title: Why the exact computation is cheap
text:
3. So a calibration takes milliseconds
TSMM needs the mean and variance of K_J and their derivatives, each one pass over that grid, and Newton needs about six passes. The badges below time it in this browser.



Because a calibration costs milliseconds, J and mu_K can be swept freely: the “Sweep” button calibrates 150 targets at once. MCMC is still needed to fit the model to data (the paper’s simulation admitted 57,151 fits, each started with four chains of 12,000 iterations), but not to choose the prior.






The gamma-mixing widget is the same file as on the Gamma mixing page (catalog C-12), mounted here with a different starting prior. Times vary by device; they are medians of five runs after a warm-up.



Standalone versions: embed/bernoulli-sum.html (for example ?J=500&alpha=1) and embed/timing-badges.html.

title: The workflow, step by step
text:
The paper’s workflow turns a statement about the number of clusters into a checked prior in six steps. Each step links to the page where you can do it yourself. Press “Fill in the J = 50 example” to see the paper’s numbers travel through the steps.






Inputs and policy are fixed first. J, the target mean and variance for K_J, the .40 trigger, the .25 soft target, the lambda grid and the separate .25 hard bound are all set before any model is fitted.
With the J = 50 example the trigger fires. TSMM matches (5, 10) exactly with Gamma(1.4082, 1.0770), but its Pr(W_SB > .5) is .497, above .40. The Dual-Anchor rule then picks lambda = .30: Gamma(2.3158, 1.4204), .398, with E K_50 = 5.88.
The hard bound is reported, not substituted. Gamma(5.2745, 2.3059) reaches .250 at E K_50 = 7.49; it belongs next to the primary prior as a sensitivity analysis.

To write the prior up, use the reporting checklist. Every tool behind the steps is listed on the Part 4 overview.

title: Same default, different J
text: A default hyperprior on the concentration parameter, such as the “vague” Gamma(1, 1), is usually chosen once and reused for every study. In Chinese-restaurant terms, alpha is the pseudo-count of “tables not yet seen”: the chance that the n-th unit opens a new table is alpha / (alpha + n - 1). The same alpha therefore implies more tables when there are more units, roughly E(alpha) log J. The size of the table a random unit joins does not work that way: its tail, Pr(W_SB > .5) = (b / (b + log 2))^a, involves no J at all.

title: Same default, different J
text:
How to read it

Panel A. Under Gamma(1, 1) the expected number of clusters is 4.16 at J = 50, 4.84 at J = 100 and 7.82 at J = 2000: the same “vague” default says something different about heterogeneity in a 50-school study and in a 2000-site registry.
Panel B. The majority-mass tail is flat: .591 for Gamma(1, 1) at every J.
Panel C (M-02). The “conservative” literature defaults Gamma(1, 3) and Gamma(2, 4) have a smaller E(alpha), so they imply fewer clusters, but a larger chance that a randomly chosen unit sits in a cluster holding more than half of the population: .812 and .726, against .591 for Gamma(1, 1). Switch Focus to compare.
The dotted guides mark the three applications in the paper: Bangert-Drowns (J = 48 studies), STAR (J = 79 schools) and the vocabulary checklist (N = 500 respondents).







K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units. W_SB is the size-biased first weight: the share of the cluster that a randomly chosen unit belongs to. It is not the largest weight. The 90% band is computed live for J ≤ 500; beyond that it is read from values precomputed with the DPprior R package.



Try a custom Gamma(a, b) with the sliders, or open the standalone version: embed/defaults-drift.html (for example ?a=1&b=3 starts the custom prior at Gamma(1, 3)).

title: Part 3 · What default hyperpriors imply
text: Every rule for choosing the Gamma(a, b) hyperprior on alpha answers one question and leaves another open. Read through two lenses at once, the count (K_J, the number of fitted components among the J units) and the weights (W_SB, the share of the cluster that a randomly chosen unit belongs to), each published rule says something its users did not ask for. Select a year for its one-line error, the evidence and a link to its explorer.

title: Part 3 · What default hyperpriors imply
text:
The story in six steps

The vague default. Gamma(1, 1) is vague about alpha, not about clusters. The expected count drifts with the design (E K_J = 4.16 at J = 50, 6.44 at J = 500) while a random unit’s chance of sitting in a majority-mass cluster stays at .591 for every J. The “conservative” defaults Gamma(1, 3) and Gamma(2, 4) raise that chance to .812 and .726. See Same default, different J and What Gamma(1, 1) actually says.
DORO (Dorazio, 2009) projects onto a flat count target. A Gamma mixture cannot be flat: the closest one is a spike at one cluster plus a hump near n, the gap grows with n, and the prior ends up expecting about n / 2 clusters. See the DORO explorer.
SCAL (Murugiah & Sweeting, 2012) fixes two count tails at every sample size, so the prior probability of a single cluster stays at .34 forever, while the weights are left to chance. Its shortcut a = b = exp(−0.033 m) collapses: at m = 100, P(K = 1) = .834. See the SCAL explorer.
SSI (Vicentini & Jermyn, 2025; the paper’s SSI-Weight) fixes the weights and never mentions J, so the expected count grows without bound: 6.44 clusters at J = 25, 20.9 at J = 5000. See the SSI explorer.
Other defaults. The quasi-degenerate Gamma(eps, eps) looks flat on the log scale and expects a single cluster; the K_n-diffuse priors of the 1990s rule out a dominant cluster; the Jeffreys prior piles mass on one cluster and on all singletons; the Stirling-gamma prior pins E(K_m) but leaves the weights unexamined. See other defaults.
The method map. Placed on one plane (expected count against the majority-mass probability), the rules show that one alpha cannot buy few clusters and little dominance for free. The DPprior Dual-Anchor makes that trade explicit at the design J. See the method map.

title: DORO, SCAL and SSI side by side
text:
Each rule below solves a reasonable-sounding problem. Read in the count view and the weight view together, each one also says something else.






DORO-Unif (after Dorazio, 2009) chooses Gamma(a, b) to minimise the Kullback–Leibler divergence from a flat count target, here on {1, …, 2 mu_K − 1}. A Gamma-mixed count distribution is hump-shaped, so the best it can do still puts about .07 on a single cluster and leaks about .07 beyond the target’s support (J = 100, mu_K = 5: Gamma(2.434, 2.461)). The paper keeps it only as an external reference because the fit fails its adequacy checks.
SCAL (Murugiah & Sweeting, 2012) fixes P(K_m = 1) = .34 and P(K_m ≥ ⌈2 ln m⌉) = .15 at every sample size m. The prior probability of complete homogeneity therefore never moves off .34. Their shortcut a = b = exp(−0.033 m) does move: at m = 100 it gives P(K = 1) = .834, a near-certain single cluster.
SSI-Weight fixes the weight tails, Pr(W_SB > .5) = .25 and Pr(W_SB > .9) = .05, with no count target: Gamma(2.179, 0.780). The expected number of clusters then grows from 6.44 at J = 25 to 20.9 at J = 5000.
Vague Gamma(1, 1), for comparison, gives P(K_100 = 1) = .168 and Pr(W_SB > .5) = .591.







All four panels are prior statements. K_J is the number of fitted components among the J units (m in SCAL’s notation). The (a, b) values come from r-export/02_methods_catalog.R (DPprior 2.0.0); probabilities are recomputed on the page. The stale value .824 for the SCAL shortcut came from a coarse quadrature; the correct value is .834.



Standalone version: embed/method-problems-strip.html (for example ?J=500 for DORO at the vocabulary size).

title: SCAL: clamped count tails, free weights
text:
Murugiah and Sweeting (2012) calibrate the Gamma hyperprior by two count probabilities that they carry to every sample size m: P(K_m = 1) = .34 and P(K_m ≥ ⌈2 ln m⌉) = .15, the values a Gamma(1, 1) gives at m = 6. For each m the two equations are solved for (a, b). The explorer solves them live and shows what the rule does not fix.





What to look for:

The two tails never move. Whatever m you choose, the red bar stays at .34 and the gold tail at .15: the prior probability of complete homogeneity is .34 for 6 units and for

At m = 100 the exact solution is Gamma(0.401, 0.364), with E K_100 = 4.77. Because the upper threshold ⌈2 ln m⌉ is an integer, the solved (a, b) jump each time it steps up (m = 8, 13, 21, 34, 55 and 91).

The weights are not part of the rule. Pr(W_SB > .5) is .590 at m = 6 and .652 at m = 100, above the vague Gamma(1, 1)’s .591. The tabulated m = 100 values, Gamma(0.403, 0.370), give E K = 4.74, Pr(W_SB > .5) = .654 and tails .340 and .148 (they are the exact solution rounded to three decimals).
The shortcut collapses. The published approximation a = b = exp(−0.033 m) tracks the solution up to about m = 25 and then falls toward zero: at m = 100 it is Gamma(0.0369, 0.0369), with P(K = 1) = .834 and E K = 2.97. That is the quasi-degenerate prior of other defaults.







Prior statements only; K_m is the number of fitted components among the m units. The (a, b) are solved in the browser by scalSolve (Newton on log a and log b); the R solution in verification/golden/solvers.csv agrees to 1e-9. Tabulated values: Vicentini and Jermyn (2025), Table 2. The curves under the chart are solved at m = 6, 8, …, 100 after the page loads; open circles mark the tabulated (a, b).



Standalone version: embed/scal-explorer.html (for example ?n=25, or ?preset=shortcut to overlay the shortcut).

title: SSI: fixed weights, a count that never stops growing
text:
Vicentini and Jermyn (2025) choose the Gamma hyperprior from statements about the weights, never about the number of units. The paper’s SSI-Weight comparator does the same with two tail probabilities: Pr(W_SB > .5) = .25 and Pr(W_SB > .9) = .05, which give Gamma(2.179, 0.780). A plausible weight judgment then implies a count that depends on J alone.





What to look for:

The weights do not move with J. The density on the left is the same for 25 units and for 5000; so are its two shaded tails, .250 and .050.
The count does. E K_J = 6.44 at J = 25, 10.05 at J = 100, 14.47 at J = 500 and 20.9 at J = 5000: “six groups among 25 sites, twenty-one among 5000”. Above J = 500 the widget shows E K_J only (digamma path); the 90% band needs the full pmf.
Other weight-only rules behave the same way. Vicentini and Jermyn’s exemplars Gamma(1.814, 1.036) (equal thirds on alpha ≤ 1, 1 < alpha ≤ 2, alpha > 2) and Gamma(1, 0.693) (half the mass on alpha ≤ 1) give E K_100 = 7.26 and 6.15, and both grow with J. Set your own two tails to see which pairs a Gamma can meet at all.
A-10: the truth outside the interval. In the paper’s simulation (J = 100, weak information I = 0.2, 200 replications per cell) SSI-Weight gives posterior means of 3.41, 3.42 and 3.39 clusters when the truth is K* = 5, 10 and 30. The average 95% interval runs from 1 to about 13.8, so it covers 5 and 10 every time and 30 never (coverage 0).







Prior statements, except the A-10 overlay, which shows posterior summaries from the paper’s simulation (data/released/headline_primary.json, grand-mean prior N(0, 1), CC BY 4.0). K_J is the number of fitted components among the J units. SSI-Weight is solved in the browser by ssiSolve (bisection on log b); the R solution (pcv_solve_ssi) agrees to 1e-12.
